name: Marco Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Marco. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to tech firms, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a sales negotiator at Brightwell Homes, which has four branches round the suburbs, and I'm in the one by the retail park. Mornings I'm on the phone chasing buyers who've viewed, afternoons I'm doing viewings on family houses, three-beds mostly. The bit I like is when a first-time buyer finally gets an offer accepted and you hear them nearly cry down the phone.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The negotiating, if I'm honest. Helen, my branch manager, can push a vendor up five grand without breaking a sweat, and I still go red when a seller shouts at me. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy up my emails, because my writing isn't great, but I'm still learning the actual craft of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a better spellcheck, that's all. At work we'd have a laugh about all the people who said agents would be gone by 2030. Online I probably wouldn't bother saying much, I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I'm not the sharpest negotiator yet, so a few years of things staying normal gives me time to actually get good. Sam, my partner, and I own our flat with a small mortgage and we've got a decent pot saved, so money isn't the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Brightwell and ask Helen if I can sit in on her harder negotiations. I'd keep using the email tool when it helps. And I'd keep overpaying the mortgage a bit each month, which we already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. Maybe a little bored by how normal it all is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money isn't the worry. Is there anything in that world that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly whether I ever get good at the hard calls. Last month a seller on Elm Grove swore at me because I passed on a low offer, and I didn't sleep. That's a me problem, not an AI problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the email tool actually do for you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes my messy notes after a viewing and turns them into a polite email to the vendor. My writing used to go out full of mistakes. Now it reads like a grown-up sent it, and Helen stopped correcting me.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **better spellcheck**, nothing more.
I'd laugh at work about predictions that **agents would vanish**.
think: A few normal years give me **time to get good** at negotiating.
With a **small mortgage** and savings, money isn't the worry.
do: **Ask Helen** to let me sit in on her hard negotiations.
Keep using the **email tool** when it helps tidy my notes.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** a little each month.
S0.quote: A seller on Elm Grove swore at me because I passed on a low offer, and I didn't sleep. That's a me problem, not an AI problem.
fieldNote: His main worry is his own **confidence** on hard calls, not technology.
He already uses AI for **emails** in a quiet, practical way.
Owning a flat with a **small mortgage** makes this world feel secure.

steps.text: Sit in on the branch manager's hardest vendor negotiations
Keep overpaying the flat's mortgage a little each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared, not just turned into bigger bonuses for whoever owns Brightwell. If software does half the admin at my agency, give people a four-day week. Don't sack the admin team. I'd say that online and probably at the Christmas do after two drinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the juniors who only book viewings and write brochures are in trouble. I'm a bit more than that because I do viewings and I talk to buyers, but I'm not the best at it yet. So I'd say I'm okay, but I'd want to be better at the human parts before they look at who to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the training the company offers on the new tools, once a couple of colleagues had tried them and they worked. I'd push hard on getting better at negotiating, maybe pay for a course myself. And I'd keep putting money away, because we've got no kids yet and it's the easiest time to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, like the floor's tilting slowly. Not falling, just tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kerry, who does the brochures and books all the viewings for the branch. She's brilliant, she knows every key on the board, but her whole job is the stuff the card says goes first. I'd want Brightwell to retrain her into a negotiator before they think about letting her go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for colleagues to try the tools first. Isn't that risky if they're moving fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I've seen tools come in and go out again in six months. I'd rather be second than first and wasting my evenings. If Josh at the next desk says something saves him an hour, I'll be on it the next morning.

say: I'd say AI gains should fund a **four-day week**, not bigger owner bonuses.
I'd argue the **admin team** should be retrained, not sacked.
think: Juniors who only **book viewings** and write brochures are in trouble.
I'm safer because I do **viewings**, but I need to improve fast.
do: **Take the company training** on new tools once colleagues prove them.
Pay for a **negotiation course** myself this year.
Keep **saving** while there are no kids yet.
S1.quote: If software does half the admin at my agency, give people a four-day week. Don't sack the admin team.
fieldNote: He separates the **booking and brochure** jobs from his own viewing work.
His instinct is to **share gains** with workers through shorter weeks.
He worries about **Kerry (the branch admin)** more than himself.

steps.text: Take Brightwell's training on the new tools once colleagues vouch for them
Pay for an evening negotiation skills course
Keep putting a fixed sum into savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency help, like furlough was during the pandemic, but for people whose jobs vanish. I'd be signing everything and probably going to my first ever march. At work I'd say it straight to Helen: are we all going?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think the job goes. The parts I'm proud of, reading a buyer, talking a vendor down, AI could do all of it by phone and email by 2028, and probably better than me. Viewings could hang on for a few years until the robots in 2031, but no one pays a negotiator's wage for opening doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month, I'd sit down with Sam and work out how long our savings cover the mortgage, which I think is well over a year. Sam's teaching might last longer, so we'd lean on that. I'd look at hands-on jobs with a few years in them, like training as a building surveyor, where you're climbing into lofts and checking damp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, a real knot in my stomach. And angry that it would hit before anyone had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why surveying rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Faisal was a surveyor and I used to go round with him in the holidays. You're on ladders, poking at walls, smelling for damp. The thinking AI could write a survey report, but someone has to get into the loft, at least until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sam that we're lucky, we own most of the flat and we've got savings. Then I'd say I'm sorry, because I know the plan was for me to earn more so we could start a family. That plan would have to wait.

say: I'd call for **emergency job support**, like pandemic furlough.
I'd go on my **first march** and ask my manager straight out.
think: Reading buyers and **talking vendors down** would be AI work by 2028.
Viewings last only until **robots in 2031**, and won't pay a wage.
do: **Work out with Sam** how long savings cover the mortgage.
**Lean on Sam's teaching** income while it lasts.
Train as a **building surveyor**, where the work is hands-on.
feel: **Scared**, with a knot in the stomach.
**Angry** that it comes before any plan.
S2.quote: The thinking AI could write a survey report, but someone has to get into the loft, at least until 2031.
fieldNote: He reads the **robot gap** carefully and picks hands-on work to buy time.
His uncle's **surveying** gives him a ready, familiar escape route.
Starting a **family** is the plan he'd postpone.

steps.text: Map how many months savings cover the mortgage with Sam
Rely on Sam's teaching salary while retraining
Start a building surveying apprenticeship within months
Postpone plans to start a family with Sam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's actually use them. I'd push for proper retraining funds and for agencies like Brightwell to give staff notice of what's being automated. I'd say that online and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get maybe three good years at Brightwell, and then the squeeze starts. Five years is enough to learn something new, though. I'd still be young, only 32, when AGI lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time surveying course next year, evenings and weekends, and keep working at Brightwell while I do it. I'd try the AI tools properly too, because they'd help me write reports later. And we'd still keep the savings strong and not move to a bigger place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a to-do list. That helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to start a family in that window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, actually, but later in it. Sam wants kids and so do I. I'd want to be qualified first, so maybe around 2029, which is cutting it fine but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be giving up to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My Saturdays, mostly. Giving up my Saturday five-a-side with the lads from school would hurt more than paying for the surveying course. The money I can find.

say: I'd say five years should be **used**, not wasted.
I'd push for agencies to give staff **notice of automation**.
think: I'd get about **three good years** before the squeeze starts.
At **32** when it lands, I'm young enough to switch.
do: **Start part-time surveying** studies next year while still working.
**Learn the AI tools** properly to help with future reports.
**Delay a bigger home** and keep savings strong.
S3.quote: Giving up my Saturday five-a-side with the lads from school would hurt more than paying for the surveying course.
fieldNote: The five-year window turns fear into a **study plan**.
He links **family timing** directly to his retraining.
His **steady** style shows: he'd learn tools once they help his next job.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time surveying course next autumn
Use AI tools daily to draft vendor reports
Stay in the current flat rather than buy a bigger one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disaster if politicians sit on it. I'd say that at work and online. I'd probably join a union too, even though agents don't usually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel quite settled. Ten years is time to become a qualified surveyor and have a few years' experience before the AI arrives. And robots wouldn't be good enough for lofts until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brightwell another couple of years and improve as a negotiator, because that's good money. Then I'd start surveying around 2028 or 2029. We'd likely start a family in that time too, since the plan would be clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit uneasy, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why join a union if you'd feel settled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be fine but Kerry might not be, and loads of people like her. A union could push for retraining pay and notice periods. It costs me a few quid a month to help someone else, and that's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change right now, in 2026, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start chatting to surveyors I know, like my uncle's old firm, and ask what the job looks like in ten years. I'd rather know now than learn the wrong thing. That's free and it'd take me a couple of coffees.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if politicians don't waste it.
I'd **join a union**, even though agents rarely do.
think: Ten years is enough to **qualify as a surveyor** and gain experience.
Robots won't manage **lofts until 2039**, giving extra years.
do: **Stay at Brightwell** a couple of years to improve negotiating.
**Talk to surveyors** at my uncle's old firm about the future.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disaster if politicians sit on it.
fieldNote: He feels **secure** because the plan and savings line up.
He'd **join a union** out of fairness, not need.
He'd gather **information early**, cheaply, before committing.

steps.text: Stay at Brightwell Homes two more years building negotiating skills
Join a union and pay the monthly fee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have savings and Sam, but no time to learn a new trade before the old one goes. What would help is paid training, like an apprenticeship wage while I learn surveying, so we don't burn through the mortgage money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the AI. If a handful of companies own the AI that sells every house, they set the fees for everyone. I'd want that out in the open and regulated, like the water companies should be.

headlineQuote: If a handful of companies own the AI that sells every house, they set the fees for everyone.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old sales negotiator** at a four-branch suburban agency, still learning to handle tough vendors.
He owns a flat with his partner Sam, with a **small mortgage** and solid savings.
He uses AI **now and then** for emails and waits for colleagues to prove tools first.
His **progressive views** show in calls for shared gains, union membership and regulated AI firms.
In the faster scenarios he plans to **retrain as a surveyor**, following his uncle, and delay starting a family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to learn a new trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship wage** while he trains as a surveyor.
